content: The document titled Guidelines on Long-Acting Injectable Cabotegravir for HIV Prevention provides a systematic review of the values and preferences regarding the use of injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), including long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA), to prevent HIV infection. It was authored by Lara Lorenzetti, Nhi Dinh, Ariane van der Straten, Virginia Fonner, Kathleen Ridgeway, Michelle Rodolph, Robin Schaefer, and Rachel Baggaley, and published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2022. The systematic review aimed to assess the values, preferences, and perceptions of end-users and community members regarding the acceptability of injectable PrEP, including CAB-LA, to inform clinical guidance and global policy. This review complements a separate analysis on the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA as PrEP. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and involved a two-stage process to evaluate references against eligibility criteria. Data from included studies were organized based on acceptability constructs such as affective attitude, burden, ethicality, intervention coherence, opportunity costs, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy. The review identified 99 articles meeting inclusion criteria, with 38 undergoing rapid extraction and 61 undergoing detailed extraction. Most studies were observational, cross-sectional, or qualitative in design. Over half of the studies were conducted in North America, with men who have sex with men (MSM) being the most researched group. Most studies examined injectable PrEP in general, including hypothetical injectables or placebo products, while six studies specifically focused on CAB-LA. Regarding affective attitude, there was general interest in and preference for injectable PrEP, though notable variation existed across groups and regions. Injectable PrEP offers an opportunity to address adherence challenges associated with daily or on-demand oral PrEP dosing and may better align with the lifestyles of individuals seeking privacy, discretion, and infrequent dosing. However, end-users expressed concerns about needle fear, injection site pain and location, logistical challenges with regular appointments, and the potential for waning or incomplete protection. The review concluded that injectable PrEP should be included as part of a menu of prevention options, considering the overall preference for and interest in this method, as well as the heterogeneity in preferences across groups and regions. However, preferences for injectable PrEP may shift over time, as with other prevention options. Future research is needed to explore enacted preferences as more end-users are exposed to antiretroviral (ARV)-containing injectables rather than placebo or hypothetical products.
